title: Introduction
summary: The text covers the first sections of a paper introducing GraphRAG, a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation approach for query-focused summarization over large private text corpora. It explains that conventional vector RAG retrieves localized records and fails on global sensemaking questions requiring understanding of an entire dataset, while prior query-focused summarization methods do not scale to RAG-sized corpora. GraphRAG addresses this by using an LLM to build an entity knowledge graph, partition it into hierarchical communities of closely related entities, and generate bottom-up community summaries that capture global descriptions and insights. Queries are answered via map-reduce over community summaries, producing partial answers in parallel and then combining them into a final response. The paper reports that for global sensemaking questions over datasets around one million tokens, GraphRAG improves answer comprehensiveness and diversity over vector RAG. Evaluation uses a novel LLM-as-a-judge method where one LLM generates diverse global questions and another judges responses on predefined criteria, with GraphRAG strongly outperforming vector RAG on two real-world datasets using GPT-4. The text also notes GraphRAG is open source and integrated with LangChain, LlamaIndex, NebulaGraph, and Neo4J.

title: Background
key_items: Using Knowledge Graphs with LLMs and RAG; Adaptive benchmarking for RAG Evaluation
Using Knowledge Graphs with LLMs and RAG
2.2 Using Knowledge Graphs with LLMs and RAG
summary: The text presents GraphRAG, a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation method for global sensemaking over large text corpora. It contrasts with conventional vector RAG, which retrieves semantically similar records and cannot support queries requiring whole-corpus understanding. GraphRAG constructs an LLM-derived knowledge graph of entities and relationships, partitions it into hierarchical communities using community detection, generates bottom-up community summaries, and answers queries through map-reduce over those summaries. The main contribution is GraphRAG and its global sensemaking capability. Evaluation uses an adaptive LLM-as-a-judge technique where one LLM generates corpus-specific sensemaking questions and another compares systems; GraphRAG strongly outperforms vector RAG with GPT-4 on two datasets. GraphRAG is open source with integrations. Background topics covered include RAG and vector RAG limitations, prior advanced RAG and hierarchical indexing, LLM-based knowledge graph extraction and graph-index RAG methods, adaptive benchmarking via persona generation, and LLM-based evaluation criteria including comparative judgment and claim validation. Method details describe the pipeline from document chunking through entity/relationship extraction, graph community detection, domain-tailored and query-focused summarization, and query-time map-reduce answer generation, including chunk-size trade-offs and figure-specific stages.

title: Methods
prefix_summary: The Methods section describes the GraphRAG workflow and its evaluation. It covers building an LLM-derived graph index from source documents via text chunking, extraction of entities/relationships/claims, aggregation into a knowledge graph, hierarchical Leiden community detection, and report-like community summaries at leaf and higher levels. Query-time processing uses community summaries to generate scored parallel intermediate answers, filters zero scores, and reduces the helpful answers into a global answer, with trade-offs such as chunk size and community hierarchy level. It also addresses domain-tailored prompts, duplicate handling, entity matching, scalability, and appendices. Evaluation uses no gold standards but employs LLM-as-a-judge comparisons and claim-based validation. The community summarization and question-answering pipeline partitions communities into mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive levels; leaf summaries prioritize prominent edges/nodes/claims and higher-level summaries combine/substitute sub-community summaries within token limits. Global sensemaking questions are generated by LLM from K personas, N tasks, and M questions per user-task with K=M=N=5, producing 125 questions per dataset with podcast and news examples. Head-to-head evaluation criteria are Comprehensiveness, Diversity, and Empowerment, plus Directness as a control for concision, with no method expected to win all four. Experiments use Behind the Tech podcast transcripts (~1M tokens; 1669 chunks of 600 tokens/100-token overlap) and 2013-2023 news articles (~1.7M tokens; 3197 chunks of 600 tokens/100-token overlap), comparing GraphRAG community levels C0-C3, TS map-reduce summarization on source texts, and SS vector RAG semantic search. Context-window and answer-generation prompts are kept consistent except minor reference-style changes, and GraphRAG uses generic entity/relationship extraction with domain-tailored entity types and few-shot examples.

nodes.title: GraphRAG Workflow
key_items: Graph Communities –> Community Summaries; Community Summaries –> Community Answers –> Global Answer
Community Summaries –> Community Answers –> Global Answer
nodes.summary: The text describes GraphRAG's pipeline and evaluation. It covers an LLM-derived graph index built from source document text, including text chunking, extraction of entities, relationships, and claims, aggregation into a knowledge graph, hierarchical Leiden community detection, and report-like community summarization at leaf and higher levels. It explains query-time preparation of community summaries, parallel intermediate answer generation with helpfulness scoring, and reduction to a global answer, as well as trade-offs such as chunk size and community hierarchy level. It discusses domain-tailored prompts, duplicate handling and entity matching, scalability, and the use of appendices for details. For evaluation, it notes the lack of gold standards, use of LLM-as-a-judge comparisons and claim-based validation, and generation of global sensemaking questions through personas, tasks, and corpus-level understanding.

nodes.title: Global Sensemaking Question Generation
key_items: 3.1.6 Community Summaries → Community Answers → Global Answer
nodes.summary: The text describes GraphRAG's hierarchical community summarization and global query answering pipeline: graph communities form mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive partitions at multiple levels; each community is summarized into a report-like summary, with leaf-level summaries prioritizing prominent edges/nodes/claims and higher-level summaries combining or substituting sub-community summaries within token limits. For a query, community summaries are shuffled and chunked, mapped to scored intermediate answers (0-100, filtering zero scores), then reduced by helpfulness into a final global answer. It also describes how global sensemaking evaluation questions are generated with an LLM by creating user personas, tasks, and high-level corpus-wide questions (125 per dataset using K=M=N=5), with examples for podcast transcripts and news articles, and how answers are evaluated head-to-head for comprehensiveness, diversity, and empowerment.

nodes.title: Criteria for Evaluating Global Sensemaking
nodes.summary: The text describes an LLM prompting procedure for generating high-level global sensemaking questions from a corpus description, producing K*N*M questions from K personas, N tasks per user, and M questions per user-task; in the evaluation K=M=N=5, yielding 125 questions per dataset. It then defines head-to-head LLM evaluation criteria for global sensemaking: Comprehensiveness, Diversity, and Empowerment, plus a control criterion Directness for concision, with no method expected to win all four. Table 1 illustrates generated example users, tasks, and questions for podcast transcripts and news articles. The experiment uses two large corpora: Behind the Tech podcast transcripts chunked into 1669 x 600-token chunks with 100-token overlaps (~1M tokens) and a news article dataset from 2013-2023 chunked into 3197 x 600-token chunks with 100-token overlaps (~1.7M tokens). It compares six conditions: GraphRAG community levels C0, C1, C2, and C3; TS map-reduce summarization directly on source texts; and SS vector RAG semantic search. Context window size and answer-generation prompts are kept the same across conditions except minor reference-style changes, while the GraphRAG index uses generic entity/relationship extraction with domain-tailored entity types and few-shot examples.

title: Analysis
summary: The text covers an evaluation methodology and experimental analysis comparing global graph-based approaches, direct text summarization, and vector RAG. It introduces directness as a control criterion and describes LLM-based pairwise answer comparison with winner/tie outputs and replicates. Experiment 1 uses podcast transcripts and news article datasets, comparing six conditions: GraphRAG at community levels C0, C1, C2, and C3, a text summarization map-reduce method TS, and vector semantic search SS. It reports configuration details such as an 8k context window, 600-token graph indexing, gpt-4-turbo use, and Leiden community detection via graspologic. Experiment 2 validates comprehensiveness and diversity with claim-based metrics using Claimify and agglomerative clustering with 1 - ROUGE-L distance. Results include graph sizes, community summaries, significant wins for global approaches over vector RAG on comprehensiveness and diversity, vector RAG being most direct, and mixed empowerment findings.

title: Results
summary: The text covers GraphRAG configuration, Experiment 2 methodology, results from Experiments 1 and 2, and limitations. Configuration used an 8k token context window for community and global answer generation and a 600 token window for graph indexing; Podcast indexing took 281 minutes on a 16GB VM with an Intel Xeon Platinum CPU and public gpt-4-turbo endpoint, while Leiden community detection used graspologic. Experiment 2 validated Experiment 1 with claim-based metrics: Claimify extracted 47,075 unique factual claims averaging 31 per answer, comprehensiveness was average claim count, and diversity was average cluster count using agglomerative clustering with complete linkage and 1-ROUGE-L across thresholds. Experiment 1 produced graphs with 8,564 nodes/20,691 edges for Podcast and 15,754 nodes/19,520 edges for News. Global approaches significantly outperformed vector RAG on comprehensiveness and diversity, while vector RAG was most direct; empowerment was mixed and specific examples, quotes, and citations were judged key. Community summaries generally improved over source text summarization except root-level, and GraphRAG showed scalability advantages, especially root-level requiring over 97% fewer tokens. Experiment 2 claim-based results aligned directionally: all global conditions and TS had significantly greater comprehensiveness than SS; diversity significance varied by dataset, with Podcast global conditions significant across thresholds and News only C0 significant across all thresholds. No significant differences existed among global conditions or between global search and TS. Aggregated LLM labels matched claim-based labels in 78% of comprehensiveness and 69-70% of diversity comparisons. Limitations note evaluation was limited to two roughly 1M token corpora and sensemaking questions, requiring broader generalization and fabrication-rate comparisons such as SelfCheckGPT.

title: Discussion
summary: This text presents GraphRAG Experiment 2 results, limitations, future work, broader impacts, and conclusion. Tables 3 and 4 report claim-based comprehensiveness and diversity metrics across conditions C0, C1, C2, C3, TS, and SS. Experiment 2 shows C0-C3 and TS significantly outperform SS on comprehensiveness in both News and Podcast datasets. For diversity, all global search conditions significantly outperform SS in Podcasts across all thresholds; in News, only C0 is significant across all thresholds, though C1-C3 show directional gains. No significant differences are found among global search conditions or between global search and TS. Claim-based metrics align with aggregated LLM preferences in 78% of comprehensiveness and 69-70% of diversity non-tie comparisons. Limitations include narrow two-corpus evaluation and lack of fabrication analysis. Future work includes hybrid local/global RAG and hierarchical roll-up/drill-down. Broader impacts advise clear AI-use disclosures due to accuracy risks. The conclusion states GraphRAG improves comprehensiveness and diversity over vector RAG and is competitive with global source-text summarization at lower token cost. Acknowledgements and a GPT-4 reference are included.

title: Conclusion
summary: The text covers a results table, future work, broader impacts, conclusion, acknowledgements, references, and appendix material. Table 4 reports average cluster counts by dataset type and distance threshold for conditions C0-C3, TS, and SS, with bold values indicating the highest per row. Future work proposes local and hybrid RAG approaches, just-in-time community report generation, roll-up, and drill-down mechanisms. Broader impacts highlights risks of inaccurate answers and recommends AI-use disclosures, while positioning GraphRAG as promising for global questions versus vector RAG. The conclusion summarizes GraphRAG as combining knowledge graph generation and query-focused summarization, with reported gains in comprehensiveness, diversity, and token efficiency. Acknowledgements and references follow. Appendix A details GPT-4 prompts for entity and relationship extraction and self-reflection to improve extraction with larger chunks, including Figure 3 on HotPotQA entity detection; Appendix B is only introduced.

title: Entity and Relationship Extraction Approach
summary: This section covers an entity and relationship extraction approach for a GraphRAG pipeline. It describes default GPT-4 prompts, a multipart LLM prompt that extracts entities and relationships into delimited tuples, and a self-reflection technique to improve extraction quality. Larger chunk sizes reduce API calls but miss entities; self-reflection mitigates this by feeding extracted entities back to the LLM, forcing a yes/no missed-entity check via logit bias, and iteratively 'gleaning' missing entities up to a set maximum. It reports that this enables larger chunks without quality loss or noise, with Figure 3 showing HotPotQA entity detection trends across chunk sizes and self-reflection iterations, and ends with a 'B Example Community Detection' heading.

title: Example Community Detection
key_items: A Entity and Relationship Extraction Approach
summary: The text covers GraphRAG's entity and relationship extraction approach using GPT-4 prompts, including entity extraction via a multipart prompt and relationship output. It explains self-reflection prompting, its use to overcome fewer entity extractions in larger chunks by gleaning missed entities up to a maximum number of iterations, and presents a figure on entity references detected by chunk size and iteration count. It also describes a community detection example using the Leiden algorithm on MultiHop-RAG with hierarchical community levels, and context window selection experiments showing that an 8k token window performed best on comprehensiveness and comparably on diversity and empowerment, leading to a fixed 8k context for final evaluation.

title: Context Window Selection
summary: The text includes a figure caption describing graph community detection with the Leiden algorithm over the MultiHop-RAG dataset, showing hierarchical entity communities at Level 0 and Level 1. It then covers context window selection experiments comparing 8k, 16k, 32k, and 64k token windows, finding that the 8k context size performs best for comprehensiveness and comparably for diversity and empowerment, leading to its use in final evaluation. Finally, it presents an example answer comparison for a news dataset question, where Graph RAG is judged better on comprehensiveness, diversity, and empowerment, while Naive RAG is judged better on directness.

title: Example Answer Comparison
summary: The text contains an example answer comparison for a News article dataset, showing a question about public figures repeatedly mentioned in entertainment articles. It compares a Graph RAG answer that categorizes public figures across broad entertainment sectors with a Naïve RAG answer that names specific individuals such as Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce. LLM-generated evaluations assess the answers on comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and directness, with Graph RAG winning the first three criteria and Naïve RAG winning directness. The text then presents system prompts: E.1 Element Instance Generation, which instructs extracting entities and relationships from text with specified formats, delimiters, and examples; and E.2 Community Summary Generation, which defines the assistant's role in information discovery for entities within a network.

title: System Prompts
prefix_summary: The System Prompts section collects prompt and instruction templates from appendices E and F. It covers E.1 element/entity-relationship extraction from documents, E.2 structured JSON community report generation with impact ratings and grounding rules, E.3 community answer generation synthesizing analyst reports while preserving modality and data references, and E.4 global answer generation for table-based questions with citation and response formatting rules. It also includes a sample community report about Verdant Oasis Plaza and the Unity March, a relative answer-assessment prompt returning JSON winner/reasoning, and four evaluation criteria: comprehensiveness, diversity, directness, and empowerment.

nodes.title: Element Instance Generation
nodes.summary: The text includes two system prompt sections under "E System Prompts." E.1 Element Instance Generation gives a goal, steps, formatting rules, an example, and a real-data template for extracting entities and relationships from a text document. E.2 Community Summary Generation begins a role prompt that defines the assistant's purpose in helping a human analyst perform information discovery about entities in a network. The chunk also includes the page number 21.

nodes.title: Community Summary Generation
nodes.summary: The text contains three system prompt templates. E.1 extracts entities and relationships from documents using defined entity/relationship fields, tuple formatting, delimiters, and examples. E.2 generates a structured JSON community report from entities, relationships, and claims, with required sections, a 0-10 impact rating, findings, and data-reference grounding rules. E.3 generates question answers by synthesizing ranked analyst reports and general knowledge while preserving modal verbs and data references and avoiding unsupported content.

nodes.title: Community Answer Generation
nodes.summary: The text describes a community revolving around Verdant Oasis Plaza, which serves as the central location for the Unity March. The plaza is the common link connecting Harmony Assembly, Unity March, and Tribune Spotlight. Harmony Assembly organizes the march, Unity March is a significant event shaping community dynamics, and Tribune Spotlight reports on it, potentially amplifying its impact. The impact severity rating is 5.0, considered moderate because of the possible unrest or conflict during the march.

nodes.title: Global Answer Generation
nodes.summary: The text is a collection of prompt/instruction templates for answer generation and evaluation. It provides citation and response formatting rules: do not mention multiple analysts, cite only supported data using report ids (max 5 plus '+more', ids not indexes), omit unsupported information, preserve modal verbs, and begin answers with a helpfulness score. It includes an E.4 Global Answer Generation role/goal for answering table-based questions, an F.1 Relative Assessment Prompt for comparing two answers and returning a JSON winner/reasoning, and F.2 definitions of four evaluation criteria: comprehensiveness, diversity, directness, and empowerment. The chunk ends with page number 25.

title: Evaluation Prompts
key_items: F Evaluation Prompts F.1 Relative Assessment Prompt
summary: The text covers evaluation prompts and statistical analysis for comparing answer quality. It provides an F.1 relative assessment prompt instructing an assistant to grade two answers using specified criteria and return JSON with a winner and reasoning. It then defines F.2 metrics: comprehensiveness, diversity, directness, and empowerment, with explanations and examples. Finally, Section 25G describes Table 6 pairwise comparisons of six conditions (C0, C1, C2, C3, TS, SS) across these four metrics over 125 questions and two datasets, using a 100/0/50 scoring system averaged over five runs, Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction, and reporting means, Z-values, and p-values for Podcast Transcripts and News Articles.

title: Statistical Analysis
summary: Table 6 reports pairwise comparisons of six conditions (C0, C1, C2, C3, TS, SS) across four metrics (Comprehensiveness, Diversity, Empowerment, Directness) for 125 questions from two datasets (Podcast Transcripts and News Articles). Each comparison was scored per question and metric by assigning 100 to the winner, 0 to the loser, and 50 to each in ties, with scores averaged over five evaluation runs. Because Shapiro-Wilk tests indicated non-normal data, non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used with Holm-Bonferroni correction; significant corrected p-values are bolded. The table lists Mean 1, Mean 2, Z-values, and p-values for all condition pairs, metrics, and datasets.
